Individuals who do not have British citizenship and who wish to move to the UK will need to follow existing visa rules and pay the Immigration Health Surcharge, where applicable, to avoid charges.

Those granted permission to enter the UK as a visitor for 6 months or less, and those without lawful immigration status, remain directly chargeable for healthcare provided by the NHS. Migrants who are not entitled to access healthcare are charged at 150% of the cost of treatment.

For example, if an individual is pregnant, not a Chagossian with British citizenship and has not paid the Immigration Health Surcharge, they would be expected to cover the full cost of giving birth in an NHS hospital. These costs typically start at £7,500 (Rs 421,875.00).

Part 2: Living in the UK

This section provides practical information about services and support you may need after arriving in the UK.

As a British citizen living in the UK, you can live and work in the UK free of immigration controls and will be entitled to certain types of support from the British state.

6. Emergency services

Call 999 if someone is in immediate danger or there is a serious emergency. The operator will ask whether you need the police, fire service or an ambulance.

Police

Call 999 to report an emergency, such as an assault or a crime in progress. Call 101 to report a non-emergency crime or seek non-urgent police assistance.

Fire

To report a fire, call 999 and ask for the fire service.

Medical emergencies

Call 999 and ask for an ambulance if someone has a serious or life-threatening illness or injury. You can also attend an Accident and Emergency department at a local hospital.

Children

The UK takes the safety and wellbeing of children very seriously. If you are concerned about a child, you can contact:

NSPCC: 0808 800 5000 or help@nspcc.org.uk

Childline: 0800 1111

if you believe a child is at immediate risk of harm, call 999 and ask for the police

7. Accommodation and homelessness

If you are homeless or at risk of losing your accommodation after moving to the UK, contact your local council as soon as possible. The council can assess your circumstances and explain what assistance may be available.

Depending on your circumstances, this may include advice, emergency accommodation, help to find longer-term accommodation or support to remain in your current accommodation.

You can also access independent housing advice through organisations such as:

Homelessness charity Shelter: Shelter - The housing and homelessness charity - Shelter England

Citizens Advice Scotland: If you’re homeless or at risk of homelessness - Citizens Advice

8. Healthcare

The service you should use depends on how urgently you need medical help. For routine healthcare, register with a GP (doctor) as soon as possible after arriving in the UK. Your GP is usually the first place to go for physical and mental health concerns, prescriptions, vaccinations, maternity care, and referrals to specialist services. Pharmacies can also provide advice and treatment for minor health conditions.

If you need medical advice or treatment that cannot wait for a GP appointment but is not an emergency, contact NHS 111. They can provide advice, arrange an interpreter if needed, and direct you to the most appropriate service, such as a doctor or an Urgent Treatment Centre.

In an emergency, if someone’s life is at risk or you do not feel able to keep yourself or someone else safe, call 999 immediately. Emergency services are available 24 hours a day.

Registering with a doctor (GP)

A General Practitioner (GP) is usually your first point of contact for physical and mental health concerns. GP appointments are free through the NHS, and GPs can provide treatment, prescriptions, health advice and referrals to specialist services. We recommend that you and your family register with a GP as soon as possible after arriving in the UK.

England, Wales and Northern Ireland: more information available here: Register with a GP surgery

Scotland: more information available here: Registering with a GP practice

Accessing medication

Your GP can advise where to collect prescribed medicines. You can also find local pharmacies here: Find a pharmacy.

Pharmacies can provide medicines and advice on minor health conditions. Some people, including those with certain medical conditions and eligible pregnant women or new mothers, may qualify for free prescriptions. Speak to your GP for advice.

Maternity care and services

NHS maternity services are available during pregnancy and after birth. Whether treatment is free will depend on your eligibility for free NHS hospital treatment. Contact a GP or maternity service as soon as you know that you are pregnant.

More information available here: Pregnancy and birth

Maternity exemption certificates: NHSBSA guidance

Scotland: Ready, Steady, Baby

Mental health and wellbeing support

If you are experiencing mental health difficulties, support is available through your GP, NHS mental health services, NHS Talking Therapies, and local support services.

NHS mental health information: NHS Mental Health

NHS Talking Therapies: Find a Talking Therapies service

Local support services: Hub of Hope

Confidential emotional support is also available through:

Samaritans: 08457 90 90 90

Shout: Text 85258

British Red Cross (support in over 200 languages): 0808 196 3651

Mind (support in over 170 languages): 0300 123 3393

Nation-specific support:

England: Mind England

Wales: Mind Cymru

Scotland: Support in Mind Scotland and NHS Inform Mental Health

Northern Ireland: Minding Your Head and Lifeline (0808 808 8000)

Eye care

Opticians provide eye tests, glasses and contact lenses. Charges apply unless you qualify for state support. In Scotland, NHS-funded eye examinations are free for all residents.

More information available here: Opticians and sight tests.

Dentistry and dental care services

Further education and skills

Further education (FE) includes courses and training after secondary school that are not part of a university degree. For young people aged 14 to 19, information on courses and qualifications is available here: Courses and qualifications for 14- to 19-year-olds.

Apprenticeships

An apprenticeship lets you earn a salary while gaining qualifications and training. Apprenticeships typically last between 1 and 6 years, depending on the programme and your experience. To start an apprenticeship in England, you must:

be aged 16 or over

not be in full-time education

live in England

British citizens moving to the UK may be eligible for apprenticeship funding if they meet the relevant criteria. More information is available here:

Apprenticeships

Funding rules for apprenticeships

Wales: Apprenticeships - GOV.WALES

Scotland: Apprenticeships.scot

14. Adult education

Adult education and English language learning

British citizens moving to England may also be eligible for courses to improve their English, maths and IT skills, some of which may be funded. More information is available here: Improve your English, maths and IT skills.

If you already have English language skills, information on proving your ability through a Secure English Language Test (SELT) is available here: Prove your English language abilities with a SELT.

For information on funding and support in Scotland, see: Student Awards Agency Scotland (SAAS).

Online language-learning tools may provide additional opportunities to practise English. These should complement, rather than replace, formal English language teaching where this is needed: Duolingo

Information on further education courses and funding for adults is available here: Further education courses and funding.

Higher education

Higher education includes courses such as diplomas, foundation degrees, bachelor’s degrees and postgraduate qualifications, usually undertaken at universities, colleges and specialist institutions. Most courses can be searched and applied for online, and you will normally need to be aged 18 or over. Information on study options and applications is available here: Study in the UK - British Council

Higher education providers set their own admissions requirements, so you should contact the institution directly if you have questions about a course. Tuition fees apply in England. British citizens moving to the UK are eligible for home fee status, meaning they do not pay international fees. Eligibility for financial support towards tuition fees may depend on meeting residence requirements.

15. Driving in the UK

You must have motor insurance to drive on UK roads. The minimum legal requirement is third-party insurance, which covers damage or injury caused to other people, vehicles, animals or property.

To apply for a provisional driving licence, you must:

be at least 15 years and 9 months old

have lived legally in the UK for at least 185 days in the previous 12 months

meet the required eyesight standards, including being able to read a number plate from 20 metres away. More information is available here: Driving eyesight rules.

16. Safety, discrimination and domestic abuse

Discrimination is illegal in the UK. You must not be treated unfairly because of characteristics such as age, disability, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation, transgender identity, pregnancy or maternity, or marriage and civil partnership. This protection applies in areas such as employment, housing, healthcare and access to services.

If you are a victim of crime

Everyone in the UK has the right to protection from crime. If you are a victim of, or witness to, a crime, contact the police by calling 999 in an emergency, 101 for non-emergencies, or reporting it online.

A hate crime is a crime motivated by hostility towards a person’s race, religion, sexual orientation, disability or transgender identity. Hate crime is taken very seriously, and anyone affected is encouraged to report it.

Further information and support are available here:

UK-wide victim support: Get support as a victim of crime

England: Report It

Wales: Hate Hurts Wales

Scotland: Police Scotland: Hate Crime

Domestic abuse

Domestic abuse is a serious crime and can include physical, emotional, psychological, controlling, coercive, sexual or economic abuse. It can affect anyone and may continue after a relationship ends. Domestic abuse can also have a significant impact on children.

If you need help or support:

24-hour National Domestic Abuse Helpline: 0808 2000 247

Domestic abuse: how to get help

Citizens Advice: Domestic violence and abuse

17. Glossary

Accident and Emergency (A&E) – Hospital department providing urgent treatment for serious illness or injury, available 24 hours a day.

Child Benefit – A government payment for parents or guardians of children under 16, or under 20 if in approved education or training.

Citizens Advice – An independent charity offering free, confidential advice on issues such as benefits, debt, housing and legal matters.

Council Tax – A local tax paid by households to fund council services such as waste collection, schools and social care.

Debit Card – A bank card used to pay for goods and services directly from your bank account.

Direct Debit – An arrangement allowing organisations to collect agreed payments directly from your bank account.

Disability benefits – Financial support available to people with disabilities, including benefits, grants and tax credits.

Education – The UK education system includes:

Early Years/Nursery (under 5)

Primary Education (ages 4-11)

Secondary Education (ages 11-16)

Further Education (typically ages 16-19)
